claim: Fluctuations in arousal, controlled by subcortical neuromodulatory systems, continuously shape cortical state.
source: Fluctuations in arousal, controlled by subcortical neuromodulatory systems, continuously shape cortical state, with profound consequences for information processing.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by the overall findings of the study and references to established literature.

claim: Arousal signals have profound consequences for information processing.
source: Fluctuations in arousal, controlled by subcortical neuromodulatory systems, continuously shape cortical state, with profound consequences for information processing.
evidence: This statement is supported by the study's findings and established scientific knowledge.

claim: Traditional accounts conceptualize arousal as a homogeneous modulator of neural population activity across the cerebral cortex.
source: Traditional accounts conceptualize arousal as a homogeneous modulator of neural population activity across the cerebral cortex.
evidence: This is a statement about previous scientific views, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Recent insights point to a higher specificity of arousal effects on different components of neural activity and across cortical regions.
source: Recent insights, however, point to a higher specificity of arousal effects on different components of neural activity and across cortical regions.
evidence: This statement is supported by recent literature cited in the manuscript.

claim: Pupil size is linked to central arousal systems.
source: Exploiting the established link between pupil size and central arousal systems, we performed concurrent magnetoencephalographic (MEG) and pupillographic recordings in a large number of participants, pooled across three laboratories.
evidence: This is an established relationship in the literature, as indicated by the word 'established' and supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: The study pooled data from three laboratories.
source: Exploiting the established link between pupil size and central arousal systems, we performed concurrent magnetoencephalographic (MEG) and pupillographic recordings in a large number of participants, pooled across three laboratories.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study design.

claim: Spontaneous pupil dilations are associated with decreases in low-frequency (2–8 Hz) activity in temporal and lateral frontal cortex.
source: We found a cascade of effects relative to the peak timing of spontaneous pupil dilations: Decreases in low-frequency (2–8 Hz) activity in temporal and lateral frontal cortex, followed by increased high-frequency (>64 Hz) activity in mid-frontal regions, followed by monotonic and inverted U relationships with intermediate frequency-range activity (8–32 Hz) in occipito-parietal regions.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the data presented in the results section.

claim: Spontaneous pupil dilations are followed by increased high-frequency (>64 Hz) activity in mid-frontal regions.
source: We found a cascade of effects relative to the peak timing of spontaneous pupil dilations: Decreases in low-frequency (2–8 Hz) activity in temporal and lateral frontal cortex, followed by increased high-frequency (>64 Hz) activity in mid-frontal regions, followed by monotonic and inverted U relationships with intermediate frequency-range activity (8–32 Hz) in occipito-parietal regions.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the data presented in the results section.

claim: Pupil-linked arousal exhibits monotonic and inverted U relationships with intermediate frequency-range activity (8–32 Hz) in occipito-parietal regions.
source: We found a cascade of effects relative to the peak timing of spontaneous pupil dilations: Decreases in low-frequency (2–8 Hz) activity in temporal and lateral frontal cortex, followed by increased high-frequency (>64 Hz) activity in mid-frontal regions, followed by monotonic and inverted U relationships with intermediate frequency-range activity (8–32 Hz) in occipito-parietal regions.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the data presented in the results section.

claim: Pupil-linked arousal coincides with widespread changes in the structure of the aperiodic component of cortical population activity.
source: Pupil-linked arousal also coincided with widespread changes in the structure of the aperiodic component of cortical population activity, indicative of changes in the excitation-inhibition balance in underlying microcircuits.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the data presented in the results section.

claim: Changes in the aperiodic component of cortical population activity are indicative of changes in the excitation-inhibition balance in underlying microcircuits.
source: Pupil-linked arousal also coincided with widespread changes in the structure of the aperiodic component of cortical population activity, indicative of changes in the excitation-inhibition balance in underlying microcircuits.
evidence: This interpretation is supported by citations to previous work (Gao et al., 2017; Waschke et al., 2021) and the data presented in the study.

claim: Variations in cortical state profoundly shape information processing and cognition.
source: Variations in cortical state profoundly shape information processing and, thus, cognition (Busse et al., 2017; Fu et al., 2014; Zagha et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited references.

claim: Variations in cortical state occur continuously due to subtle fluctuations in the level of arousal, even in the absence of changes in overt behavior.
source: These variations occur continuously due to subtle fluctuations in the level of arousal, and even in the absence of changes in overt behavior (Harris and Thiele, 2011; McGinley et al., 2015b).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited references.

claim: The brainstem nucleus locus coeruleus (LC) supplies noradrenaline (NE) and is a key mediator of arousal-dependent variations.
source: Two key mediators of arousal-dependent variations are the brainstem nucleus locus coeruleus (LC), which supplies noradrenaline (NE), and the basal forebrain (BF), which supplies acetylcholine (ACh) (Harris and Thiele, 2011; Hasselmo, 1995; Lee and Dan, 2012; Steriade, 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited references.

claim: The basal forebrain (BF) supplies acetylcholine (ACh) and is a key mediator of arousal-dependent variations.
source: Two key mediators of arousal-dependent variations are the brainstem nucleus locus coeruleus (LC), which supplies noradrenaline (NE), and the basal forebrain (BF), which supplies acetylcholine (ACh) (Harris and Thiele, 2011; Hasselmo, 1995; Lee and Dan, 2012; Steriade, 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited references.

claim: It has long been thought that LC and BF nuclei are organized homogeneously and innervate cortical target regions diffusely and indiscriminately across cortical regions.
source: It has long been thought that these nuclei are organized homogeneously and innervate cortical target regions diffusely, and indiscriminately across cortical regions.
evidence: This is a statement about historical scientific views.

claim: The traditional view led to the idea that the arousal system acts as a global 'broadcast signal' and uniform controller of cortical state.
source: This has led to the idea that the arousal system acts as a global 'broadcast signal' and uniform controller of cortical state (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Harris and Thiele, 2011; Leopold et al., 2003; Turchi et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited references.

claim: Several neuronal subpopulations with distinct projection targets have been found in both the LC and BF.
source: More recently, however, this view has been challenged: Several neuronal subpopulations with distinct projection targets have been found in both the LC and BF (Chandler et al., 2013; Chandler et al., 2019; Sarter et al., 2009; Schwarz and Luo, 2015; Totah et al., 2018; Zaborszky et al., 2015; Záborszky et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited references.

claim: Pupil diameter can be used as a proxy for arousal.
source: We used pupil diameter as a proxy for arousal (Beatty, 1982; Bradshaw, 1967; Hess and Polt, 1964; Kahneman et al., 1967; Kahneman and Beatty, 1966).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited references.

claim: Pupil diameter has recently attracted interest in neuroscience as a peripheral index of how arousal influences cortical state.
source: Pupil diameter has recently attracted interest in neuroscience as a peripheral index of how arousal influences cortical state (McGinley et al., 2015b; Reimer et al., 2014; Vinck et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited references.

claim: Spontaneous changes in pupil diameter mimic the effects seen during the behavioral transition from quiet wakefulness to locomotion in rodents.
source: Spontaneous changes in pupil diameter mimic the effects seen during the behavioral transition from quiet wakefulness to locomotion in rodents (Crochet and Petersen, 2006; Niell and Stryker, 2010; Polack et al., 2013; Poulet and Petersen, 2008): suppression of low (<10 Hz) and elevation of higher frequency (>30 Hz) activity (McGinley et al., 2015b; Reimer et al., 2014; Vinck et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited references.

claim: The behavioral transition from quiet wakefulness to locomotion in rodents is associated with suppression of low (<10 Hz) and elevation of higher frequency (>30 Hz) activity.
source: Spontaneous changes in pupil diameter mimic the effects seen during the behavioral transition from quiet wakefulness to locomotion in rodents (Crochet and Petersen, 2006; Niell and Stryker, 2010; Polack et al., 2013; Poulet and Petersen, 2008): suppression of low (<10 Hz) and elevation of higher frequency (>30 Hz) activity (McGinley et al., 2015b; Reimer et al., 2014; Vinck et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited references.

claim: Fluctuations in pupil diameter under constant retinal illumination track LC-NE activity.
source: Critically, fluctuations in pupil diameter under constant retinal illumination track LC-NE activity (Breton-Provencher and Sur, 2019; de Gee et al., 2017; Joshi et al., 2016; Murphy et al., 2014; Reimer et al., 2016) as well as BF-ACh activity (Reimer et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited references.

claim: Fluctuations in pupil diameter under constant retinal illumination track BF-ACh activity.
source: Critically, fluctuations in pupil diameter under constant retinal illumination track LC-NE activity (Breton-Provencher and Sur, 2019; de Gee et al., 2017; Joshi et al., 2016; Murphy et al., 2014; Reimer et al., 2016) as well as BF-ACh activity (Reimer et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Fluctuations in pupil diameter are reflected more strongly in cholinergic activity.
source: Fluctuations in pupil diameter are reflected more strongly in cholinergic activity, whereas the rate of change in pupil diameter (i.e., its temporal derivative) is most strongly associated with noradrenergic activity (Reimer et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited reference.

claim: The rate of change in pupil diameter (i.e., its temporal derivative) is most strongly associated with noradrenergic activity.
source: Fluctuations in pupil diameter are reflected more strongly in cholinergic activity, whereas the rate of change in pupil diameter (i.e., its temporal derivative) is most strongly associated with noradrenergic activity (Reimer et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Animal research on pupil-linked arousal has mostly been limited to circumscribed sensory cortical areas in rodents.
source: Animal research has mostly been limited to circumscribed sensory cortical areas in rodents (McGinley et al., 2015a; Reimer et al., 2014; but see Shimaoka et al., 2018) and in the anterior cingulate cortex of the macaque brain (Joshi and Gold, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited references.

claim: Non-invasive MRI in humans has revealed spatially rich correlations of cortical activity with pupil-linked arousal.
source: Insights from non-invasive magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in humans, on the other hand, have revealed spatially rich correlations of cortical activity with pupil-linked arousal (Groot et al., 2021; Schneider et al., 2016; Yellin et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited references.

claim: The low temporal resolution of MRI measurements complicates direct comparisons with results from electrophysiological recordings in rodents and non-human primates.
source: However, the low temporal resolution of these measurements complicates direct comparisons with results from electrophysiological recordings in rodents and non-human primates.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of MRI, based on general knowledge of the technique.

claim: There is a lack of comprehensive understanding of which features of cortical population activity are shaped by arousal and how such effects are distributed across cortex.
source: Therefore, we still lack a comprehensive understanding of which features of cortical population activity are shaped by arousal and how such effects are distributed across cortex.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: The study assessed the covariation of spontaneous fluctuations in pupil-linked arousal and whole-head MEG recordings in resting human participants across brain regions, components of cortical activity, and temporal lags.
source: To close these gaps, we assessed the covariation of spontaneous fluctuations in pupil-linked arousal and whole-head magnetoencephalographic (MEG) recordings in resting human participants across brain regions (Figure 1), components of cortical activity (oscillatory and aperiodic), and temporal lags.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study design.

claim: The study demonstrates opposite effects of pupil-linked arousal on low- and high-frequency components of cortical population activity across large parts of the brain.
source: First, we demonstrate opposite effects of pupil-linked arousal on low- and high-frequency components of cortical population activity across large parts of the brain, similar to previously observed effects in rodent sensory cortices.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the data presented in the results section.

claim: The opposite effects of pupil-linked arousal on low- and high-frequency components occurred in a systematic temporal sequence.
source: First, we demonstrate opposite effects of pupil-linked arousal on low- and high-frequency components of cortical population activity across large parts of the brain, similar to previously observed effects in rodent sensory cortices. These distinct effects occurred in a systematic temporal sequence.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the data presented in the results section.

claim: The study uncovered nonlinear (inverted U-shaped) arousal effects in occipito-parietal cortex.
source: Second, we also uncovered hitherto unknown, nonlinear (inverted U-shaped) arousal effects in occipito-parietal cortex.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the data presented in the results section.

claim: The study identified spatially widespread correlations between pupil-linked arousal and the structure of aperiodic activity.
source: Third, we identified spatially widespread correlations between pupil-linked arousal and the structure of aperiodic activity, suggesting underlying changes in cortical excitation-inhibition balance (Gao et al., 2017; Waschke et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the data presented in the results section and cited references.

claim: The study analyzed data from concurrent whole-head MEG and pupil recordings in 81 human participants.
source: We analyzed data from concurrent whole-head MEG and pupil recordings in 81 human participants, collected at three MEG laboratories (Glasgow, UK; Hamburg & Münster, Germany).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study design.

claim: All recordings were carried out under constant illumination and in sound-attenuated environments.
source: All recordings were carried out under constant illumination and in sound-attenuated environments, thus removing fluctuations in pupil size due to changes in sensory input.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental conditions.

claim: Constant illumination and sound-attenuated environments remove fluctuations in pupil size due to changes in sensory input.
source: All recordings were carried out under constant illumination and in sound-attenuated environments, thus removing fluctuations in pupil size due to changes in sensory input.
evidence: This is a statement about the rationale for the experimental design, based on knowledge of how pupil size is affected by sensory input.

claim: Participants were instructed to keep their eyes open, while fixating and resting otherwise.
source: Participants were instructed to keep their eyes open, while fixating and resting otherwise.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental instructions.

claim: The length of individual recordings varied between 5 and 10 min.
source: The length of individual recordings varied between 5 and 10 min (see Materials and methods for further details).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: MEG and pupil recordings were highly comparable between laboratories.
source: A first control analysis of the recordings (Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2) established that they were highly comparable between laboratories, despite the differences in locations, setups, and participants.
evidence: This statement is supported by the control analysis presented in the supplementary figures.

claim: The pupil diameter time course and its temporal derivative indicate distinct (cholinergic and noradrenergic, respectively) neuromodulatory inputs to cortex.
source: Previous work in rodents suggests that this time course and its temporal derivative indicate distinct (cholinergic and noradrenergic, respectively) neuromodulatory inputs to cortex (Reimer et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited reference.

claim: In the study's data, the results were largely similar for pupil and pupil derivative.
source: In our data, the results were largely similar for pupil and pupil derivative.
evidence: This is a statement about the study's findings.

claim: Mutual information (MI) is sensitive to monotonic as well as non-monotonic associations between two signals.
source: We evaluated the strength of pupil-brain coupling across a wide range of frequency bands in MEG sensor space by means of mutual information (MI), which is sensitive to monotonic as well as non-monotonic associations between two signals (Ince et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited reference.

claim: For all three MEG laboratories, standardized-MI spectra showed similar patterns of widespread pupil-brain associations across frequencies with prominent peaks in the 8–32 Hz range.
source: For all three MEG laboratories, standardized-MI spectra showed similar patterns of widespread pupil-brain associations across frequencies with prominent peaks in the 8–32 Hz range (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: MI scalp distributions within the 8-32 Hz frequency range underpinned the commonalities between recording sites despite different MEG systems and setups.
source: MI scalp distributions within this frequency range further underpinned the commonalities between recording sites despite different MEG systems and setups (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a finding of the study, supported by the data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: Significant relationships with pupil size were evident for the low-frequency (4–8 Hz) and high-frequency (64–128 Hz) components of MEG power in all three datasets.
source: Significant relationships with pupil size were also evident for the low-frequency (4–8 Hz) and high-frequency (64–128 Hz) components of MEG power (Figure 2A) in all three datasets.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: Microsaccades led to a transient suppression of cortical activity in the 8–32 Hz range.
source: An additional control analysis found that remaining microsaccades (not captured by the regressing-out) led to a transient suppression of cortical activity in the 8–32 Hz range.
evidence: This is a finding from a control analysis, supported by the data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The microsaccade-related suppression of cortical activity in the 8–32 Hz range was not associated with any changes in pupil diameter.
source: However, this effect was not associated with any changes in pupil diameter (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from a control analysis, supported by the data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Changes of neural activity in brainstem arousal centers such as the LC generate changes in neural activity that exhibit considerable temporal lag (~500 ms in macaques) and temporal low-pass characteristics.
source: Changes of neural activity in brainstem arousal centers such as the LC generate changes in neural activity that exhibit considerable temporal lag (~500 ms in macaques) and temporal low-pass characteristics (Breton-Provencher and Sur, 2019; de Gee et al., 2017; Hoeks and Levelt, 1993; Joshi et al., 2016; Korn and Bach, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited references.

claim: Temporal smoothing in the relationship between LC activity and pupil diameter is produced by the peripheral pathways (nerves and muscles) controlling pupil motility.
source: This temporal smoothing is produced by the peripheral pathways (nerves and muscles) controlling pupil motility (Hoeks and Levelt, 1993; Korn and Bach, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited references.

claim: The effect of neuromodulatory arousal signals might occur earlier in cortical population activity than in pupil diameter.
source: Thus, one might expect the effect of neuromodulatory arousal signals to occur earlier in cortical population activity (a single synapse from LC to cortex, unless mediated by a third structure, such as the thalamus) than in pupil diameter.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the known anatomy and physiology of the arousal system.

claim: For activity in the low- (around 2–4 Hz) and high-frequency bands (around 64–128 Hz), correlation magnitudes peaked at lags of 832 ms (negative peak) and 562 ms (positive peak), respectively.
source: For activity in the low- (around 2–4 Hz) and high-frequency bands (around 64–128 Hz), correlation magnitudes peaked at lags of 832 ms (negative peak) and 562 ms (positive peak), respectively.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the data presented in Figure 3.

claim: The lags of 832 ms and 562 ms for low- and high-frequency activity were highly consistent across the three MEG sites.
source: This result was highly consistent across the three MEG sites (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding of the study, supported by the data presented in Figure 3A.

claim: The lags of 832 ms and 562 ms indicated power fluctuations that preceded corresponding variations in pupil diameter.
source: These latencies indicated power fluctuations that preceded corresponding variations in pupil diameter.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the lag data.

claim: Correlations with power fluctuations in the 8–16 Hz range peaked at a lag closer to zero (210 ms; positive peak).
source: Correlations with power fluctuations in the 8–16 Hz range, on the other hand, peaked at a lag closer to zero (210 ms; positive peak), indicating a temporally closer relationship (Figure 3A and B; see Discussion).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the data presented in Figure 3.

claim: A negative correlation between pupil diameter fluctuations and power in the low frequencies (2–4 Hz) peaked at a lag of around 900 ms, with a spatial profile that was relatively uniform across brain areas.
source: Consistent with the results obtained from sensor averages, a negative correlation between pupil diameter fluctuations and power in the low frequencies (2–4 Hz) peaked at a lag of around 900 ms, with a spatial profile that was relatively uniform across brain areas (Figure 3C, left).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: For the high frequencies (64–128 Hz), the positive peak was confined to posterior regions, with a lag similar to the low-frequency band.
source: For the high frequencies (64–128 Hz), on the other hand, the positive peak was confined to posterior regions, with a lag similar to the low-frequency band (Figure 3C, right).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: In the 8–16 Hz-range, the close-to zero-lag positive correlation dominated posterior sensors whereas anterior sensors registered a negative correlation with a peak around 1 s.
source: In the 8–16 Hz-range, the picture was more nuanced (Figure 3C, center): The close-to zero-lag positive correlation dominated posterior sensors whereas anterior sensors registered a negative correlation with a peak around 1 s.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: The correlation between pupil diameter and power in the 8–16 Hz range may have been driven by independent mechanisms that operate on distinct time scales.
source: This suggests that the correlation between pupil diameter and power in the 8–16 Hz range may have been driven by independent mechanisms that operate on distinct time scales (see Discussion).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data, suggesting a hypothesis.

claim: The lags between spontaneous fluctuations in pupil diameter and low- and high-frequency activity are consistent with previously reported lags between noradrenergic and cholinergic activity, respectively, and spontaneous pupil diameter fluctuations in rodents.
source: In summary, we identified lags between spontaneous fluctuations in pupil diameter and low- and high-frequency activity that are consistent with previously reported lags between noradrenergic and cholinergic activity, respectively, and spontaneous pupil diameter fluctuations in rodents.
evidence: This is a summary statement that compares the study's findings to previous work in rodents.

claim: Pupil-brain coupling in the intermediate 8–16 Hz range peaked with a time lag closer to maximum pupil dilation for posterior sensors.
source: In addition, we found that pupil-brain coupling in the intermediate 8–16 Hz range peaked with a time lag closer to maximum pupil dilation for posterior sensors.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's findings.

claim: The correlations in different frequency bands, and for different cortices within the intermediate frequency range, may be mediated by different neuromodulatory systems.
source: Our findings suggest that the correlations in different frequency bands, and for different cortices within the intermediate frequency range, may be mediated by different neuromodulatory systems (see Discussion).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data, suggesting a hypothesis.

claim: A lag of 930 ms was used to shift the pupil signal forward relative to the MEG signal for source-level analysis.
source: Based on previous reports (Hoeks and Levelt, 1993; Joshi et al., 2016; Reimer et al., 2016), we shifted the pupil signal 930 ms forward (with respect to the MEG signal) for this analysis.
evidence: This is a statement about the analysis method, based on previous reports.

claim: The 930 ms shift was introduced to compensate for the lag that had previously been observed between external manipulations of arousal as well as spontaneous noradrenergic activity and changes in pupil diameter.
source: We introduced this shift to compensate for the lag that had previously been observed between external manipulations of arousal (Burlingham et al., 2021; Hoeks and Levelt, 1993; Wierda et al., 2012) as well as spontaneous noradrenergic activity (Reimer et al., 2016) and changes in pupil diameter.
evidence: This is a statement about the rationale for the analysis method, based on previous reports.

claim: The 930 ms shift aligned with the lags for low- and high-frequency extrema in the cross-correlation analysis.
source: In our data, this shift also aligned with the lags for low- and high-frequency extrema in the cross-correlation analysis (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a statement about the consistency of the analysis method with the study's findings.

claim: Correlations between intrinsic pupil size and power fluctuations were frequency-dependent when averaged across all source locations.
source: Averaged across all source locations, correlations between intrinsic pupil size and power fluctuations were frequency-dependent (Figure 4A):
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: There was a robust negative correlation between pupil diameter and power in the low frequencies (2–8 Hz).
source: Consistent with findings from invasive recordings in primary visual cortex of rodents (Reimer et al., 2014; Vinck et al., 2015), we found a robust negative correlation between pupil diameter and power in the low frequencies (2–8 Hz) and a numerically small, albeit statistically robust, positive correlation in the high frequencies (between 50 and 100 Hz).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the data presented in Figure 4A and consistent with previous work in rodents.

claim: There was a numerically small, albeit statistically robust, positive correlation between pupil diameter and power in the high frequencies (between 50 and 100 Hz).
source: Consistent with findings from invasive recordings in primary visual cortex of rodents (Reimer et al., 2014; Vinck et al., 2015), we found a robust negative correlation between pupil diameter and power in the low frequencies (2–8 Hz) and a numerically small, albeit statistically robust, positive correlation in the high frequencies (between 50 and 100 Hz).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: Correlations in the low frequencies covered large parts of the brain (except for a few posterior regions).
source: Whereas the correlations in the low frequencies covered large parts of the brain (except for a few posterior regions, Figure 4B), pupil-brain coupling in other frequency ranges exhibited a spatially richer structure, with positive (8–32 Hz) and negative (>50 Hz) correlations in more occipital regions and correlations of opposite sign in more anterior sources (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: Pupil-brain coupling in the 8–32 Hz and >50 Hz frequency ranges exhibited a spatially richer structure, with positive (8–32 Hz) and negative (>50 Hz) correlations in more occipital regions and correlations of opposite sign in more anterior sources.
source: Whereas the correlations in the low frequencies covered large parts of the brain (except for a few posterior regions, Figure 4B), pupil-brain coupling in other frequency ranges exhibited a spatially richer structure, with positive (8–32 Hz) and negative (>50 Hz) correlations in more occipital regions and correlations of opposite sign in more anterior sources (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: Patterns of pupil-power correlations were highly region-specific.
source: Patterns of pupil-power correlations were highly region-specific:
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's findings, supported by the data presented in Figure 4C.

claim: Correlations in the primary visual cortex were positive within the 8–32 Hz range.
source: Correlations in the primary visual cortex were positive within the 8–32 Hz range (Figure 4C, top).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the data presented in Figure 4C.

claim: Correlations in the auditory cortex were dominated by negative correlations in the low-frequency range (<8 Hz).
source: Correlations in the auditory cortex, on the other hand, were dominated by negative correlations in the low-frequency range (<8 Hz; Figure 4C, second to top).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the data presented in Figure 4C.

claim: Somatosensory cortex exhibited negative correlations in the low and intermediate frequencies (2–16 Hz) and, at the same time, positive correlations in the high-frequency range (~64 Hz).
source: Somatosensory cortex exhibited negative correlations in the low and intermediate frequencies (2–16 Hz) and, at the same time, positive correlations in the high-frequency range (~64 Hz; Figure 4C, second to bottom).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the data presented in Figure 4C.

claim: Correlations with activity in anterior cingulate were significant across most frequencies, with a spectral pattern similar to auditory cortex.
source: Correlations with activity in anterior cingulate were significant across most frequencies, with a spectral pattern similar to auditory cortex (Figure 4C, bottom).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the data presented in Figure 4C.

claim: In the low frequencies (centered at 4 Hz), correlations were negative in the majority of source locations, with bilateral peaks in the anterior sections of the hippocampus.
source: In the low frequencies (centered at 4 Hz), correlations were negative in the majority of source locations, with bilateral peaks in the anterior sections of the hippocampus (Figure 4D, top left).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the data presented in Figure 4D.

claim: Significant positive correlations between pupil and activity in the alpha/beta range (11.3 and 19 Hz) were located in the visual cortices of both hemispheres.
source: Significant positive correlations between pupil and activity in the alpha/beta range (11.3 and 19 Hz) were located in the visual cortices of both hemispheres (Figure 4D, top right and bottom left).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the data presented in Figure 4D.

claim: Significant negative correlations were found in left and right motor and somatosensory cortices, although limited to activity in the alpha range (centered at 11.3 Hz).
source: Significant negative correlations were found in left and right motor and somatosensory cortices (Figure 4D, top right), although limited to activity in the alpha range (centered at 11.3 Hz).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the data presented in Figure 4D.

claim: Correlations with high-frequency activity (centered at 64 Hz) were non-uniform across space, with negative correlations located in visual cortices bilaterally, and positive correlations across large parts of the prefrontal cortex.
source: Similarly, correlations with high-frequency activity (centered at 64 Hz) were non-uniform across space, with negative correlations located in visual cortices bilaterally, and positive correlations across large parts of the prefrontal cortex (Figure 4D, bottom right).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the data presented in Figure 4D.

claim: Repeating the analyses for the pupil derivative yielded largely similar spatial patterns for the correlations, albeit with reduced magnitudes.
source: Repeating the analyses for the pupil derivative, we found largely similar spatial patterns for the correlations, albeit with reduced magnitudes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; see Figure 4—figure supplement 2 for statistical comparison of pupil-power and pupil-derivative-power correlations).
evidence: This is a finding of the study, supported by the data presented in the supplementary figures.

claim: McGinley et al., 2015a, reported a similar reduction when comparing pupil derivative with pupil-based correlations in rodents.
source: McGinley et al., 2015a, reported a similar reduction when comparing pupil derivative with pupil-based correlations in rodents.
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Source localization of pupil-brain coupling revealed frequency band-specific patterns of arousal influences on cortical processing.
source: Briefly summarized, source localization of pupil-brain coupling revealed frequency band-specific patterns of arousal influences on cortical processing.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's findings.

claim: While coupling with low-frequency activity was relatively uniform, coupling with intermediate- and high-frequency activity showed effects of opposite signs for different cortices, even within frequency bands.
source: While coupling with low-frequency activity was relatively uniform, coupling with intermediate- and high-frequency activity showed effects of opposite signs for different cortices, even within frequency bands, indicating that arousal has discernible effects on different sensory cortices, as well as higher-order associative regions of the human brain at rest.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's findings.

claim: Arousal has discernible effects on different sensory cortices, as well as higher-order associative regions of the human brain at rest.
source: While coupling with low-frequency activity was relatively uniform, coupling with intermediate- and high-frequency activity showed effects of opposite signs for different cortices, even within frequency bands, indicating that arousal has discernible effects on different sensory cortices, as well as higher-order associative regions of the human brain at rest.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Arousal may exert more complex influences on cortical activity that roughly follow a nonlinear, inverted U shape, known as the Yerkes-Dodson law.
source: However, arousal may exert more complex influences on cortical activity that roughly follow a nonlinear, inverted U shape, known as the Yerkes-Dodson law (Yerkes and Dodson, 1908; Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; McGinley et al., 2015b).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited references.

claim: Evidence suggests that gain of neuronal input-output functions as well as behavioral performance peak at intermediate arousal levels.
source: Evidence suggests that gain of neuronal input-output functions as well as behavioral performance peak at intermediate arousal levels (He and Zempel, 2013; McGinley et al., 2015b; Waschke et al., 2019), flanked by lower gain and performance at lower (e.g., disengagement and drowsiness) and higher arousal (e.g., stress).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited references.

claim: The relation between pupil diameter and pupil derivative with low-frequency (2–4 Hz) and high-frequency activity (64–128 Hz) was well characterized by a monotonic relationship when averaged across all source locations.
source: Focusing on three predefined frequency bands, the relation between pupil diameter and pupil derivative with low-frequency (2–4 Hz) and high-frequency activity (64–128 Hz) was well characterized by a monotonic relationship (Figure 5A, left and right) when averaged across all source locations.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the data presented in Figure 5A.

claim: Activity in the 8–16 Hz range exhibited a high degree of nonlinearity that followed an inverted U relationship.
source: In contrast, activity in the 8–16 Hz range exhibited a high degree of nonlinearity that followed an inverted U relationship (Figure 5A, center).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the data presented in Figure 5A.

claim: Inverted U relationships were exclusive to the range of 8–32 Hz.
source: The analysis revealed that inverted U relationships were exclusive to the range of 8–32 Hz (i.e., β2 significantly smaller than zero; two-tailed paired t-test; Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the data presented in Figure 5B.

claim: The inverted U relationship in the alpha band (11 Hz) peaked in the superior parietal lobule.
source: A spatially more fine-grained analysis of these effects revealed that the inverted U relationship in the alpha band (11 Hz) peaked in the superior parietal lobule (Figure 5D, center left).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the data presented in Figure 5D.

claim: The inverted U relationship mapped at a higher center frequency (19 Hz) comprised additional bilateral parietal and temporal regions.
source: The same relationship mapped at a higher center frequency (19 Hz) comprised additional bilateral parietal and temporal regions (Figure 5D, right).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the data presented in Figure 5D.

claim: There was some evidence for quadratic relationships when analyzing the pupil derivative instead of the pupil diameter, however exhibiting different spatial patterns and a less pronounced inverted U-shape for the intermediate frequency range.
source: We also found some evidence for quadratic relationships when analyzing the pupil derivative instead of the pupil diameter, however exhibiting different spatial patterns and a less pronounced inverted U-shape for the intermediate frequency range (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding of the study, supported by the data presented in the supplementary figure.

claim: Evidence for an inverted U relationship between pupil-linked arousal and band-limited cortical activity was confined to the classical alpha/beta frequency band (8–32 Hz) and parieto-occipital cortices.
source: Taken together, we found evidence for a inverted U relationship between pupil-linked arousal and band-limited cortical activity that was confined to the classical alpha/beta frequency band (8–32 Hz) and parieto-occipital cortices.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's findings.

claim: Cortical activity in the alpha/beta frequency range, and in parieto-occipital cortical regions, was maximal at medium pupil diameters that indicate intermediate optimal levels of arousal.
source: Put differently, cortical activity in this frequency range, and in the respective cortical regions, was maximal at medium pupil diameters that indicate intermediate optimal levels of arousal.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Activity in surrounding low- and high-frequency ranges showed exclusively linear effects.
source: Activity in surrounding low- and high-frequency ranges showed exclusively linear effects.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's findings.

claim: The slope of the 1/f component reflects fluctuations in attentional state.
source: The slope of the 1/f component reflects fluctuations in attentional state (Waschke et al., 2021) and has been suggested to track the ratio between excitation and inhibition (in short: E/I) in the underlying neuronal circuits (Gao et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited references.

claim: The slope of the 1/f component has been suggested to track the ratio between excitation and inhibition (E/I) in the underlying neuronal circuits.
source: The slope of the 1/f component reflects fluctuations in attentional state (Waschke et al., 2021) and has been suggested to track the ratio between excitation and inhibition (in short: E/I) in the underlying neuronal circuits (Gao et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Neuromodulators linked with the regulation of arousal have been shown to change cortical E/I.
source: As neuromodulators linked with the regulation of arousal have been shown to change cortical E/I (Martins and Froemke, 2015; Pfeffer et al., 2018; Pfeffer et al., 2021), we next investigated the relation between intrinsic fluctuations in pupil diameter (as well as its temporal derivative) and the aperiodic component in the power spectrum.
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited references.

claim: Simulations of a biologically plausible neural network show that spectral slopes extracted from the 3-40 Hz frequency range are sensitive to changes in the underlying ratio between excitation and inhibition.
source: Simulations of a biologically plausible neural network (Trakoshis et al., 2020) as well as empirical insights from optogenetic stimulations in neonatal mice (Chini et al., 2021) show that spectral slopes extracted from the chosen frequency range are in fact sensitive to changes in the underlying ratio between excitation and inhibition.
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited references.

claim: Empirical insights from optogenetic stimulations in neonatal mice show that spectral slopes extracted from the 3-40 Hz frequency range are sensitive to changes in the underlying ratio between excitation and inhibition.
source: Simulations of a biologically plausible neural network (Trakoshis et al., 2020) as well as empirical insights from optogenetic stimulations in neonatal mice (Chini et al., 2021) show that spectral slopes extracted from the chosen frequency range are in fact sensitive to changes in the underlying ratio between excitation and inhibition.
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited reference.

claim: The spectral exponent decreased strongly linearly as a function of pupil diameter.
source: The spectral exponent decreased strongly linearly as a function of pupil diameter (Figure 6A), indicative of a shallower decay of power as a function of frequency (see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the data presented in Figure 6A.

claim: The decrease in spectral exponent as a function of pupil diameter is indicative of a shallower decay of power as a function of frequency.
source: The spectral exponent decreased strongly linearly as a function of pupil diameter (Figure 6A), indicative of a shallower decay of power as a function of frequency (see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data, based on the definition of the spectral exponent.

claim: Correlating the fluctuations in the estimated spectral exponent with fluctuations in pupil diameter across all bins resulted in a significant negative correlation when averaged across all source locations.
source: We next correlated the fluctuations in the estimated spectral exponent with fluctuations in pupil diameter across all bins (i.e., without prior sorting and averaging within bins). This resulted in a significant negative correlation when averaged across all source locations (Figure 6B, gray dots), with little variability when zooming in on four regions of interest (visual cortex: mean r = –0.0278; p = 0.0014; auditory cortex: mean r = –0.0518, p = 4.5*10–10; somatosensory cortex: mean r = –0.0421, p = 1.09*10–5; anterior cingulate cortex: r = –0.0336, p = 1.09*10–5; two-tailed paired t-tests against zero).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the data presented in Figure 6B.

claim: The negative correlation between the spectral exponent and mean pupil diameter for the corresponding segment was significant in the vast majority of brain regions (8137/8799 of source locations, or 92.5%, after adjusting for a false discovery rate (FDR) of 0.1).
source: In fact, the negative correlation between the spectral exponent and mean pupil diameter for the corresponding segment was significant in the vast majority of brain regions (8137/8799 of source locations, or 92.5%, after adjusting for a false discovery rate (FDR) of 0.1; Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the data presented in Figure 6C.

claim: A correlation between spectral exponent and pupil diameter was notably absent in several extrastriate occipital cortices.
source: A correlation was notably absent in several extrastriate occipital cortices.
evidence: This is a finding of the study, supported by the data presented in Figure 6C.

claim: A similarly widespread negative correlation was found between the spectral exponent and the pupil derivative, although weaker in magnitude.
source: We found a similarly widespread negative correlation between the spectral exponent and the pupil derivative. Although weaker in magnitude, this effect additionally encompassed the entire occipital cortex and showed stronger local maxima in parietal cortices, when compared with the correlation with pupil (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-C).
evidence: This is a finding of the study, supported by the data presented in the supplementary figure.

claim: The results speak to a global effect of pupil-linked arousal on the excitation-inhibition ratio across the brain, with few potential exceptions (occipital cortices).
source: In sum, these results speak to a global effect of pupil-linked arousal on the excitation-inhibition ratio across the brain, with few potential exceptions (occipital cortices).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Minor differences between pupil- and pupil-derivative-based spatial patterns of effects on the spectral exponent may point toward the involvement of different neuromodulators.
source: Minor differences between pupil- and pupil-derivative-based spatial patterns of these effects may again point toward the involvement of different neuromodulators.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings, suggesting a hypothesis.

claim: Pupil-linked changes in the slope of the aperiodic component of the cortical power spectrum could introduce spurious changes in band-limited power.
source: Given the pupil-linked changes in the slope of the (aperiodic component of) the cortical power spectrum, one concern is that these introduced spurious changes in band-limited power (Donoghue et al., 2020), thus potentially producing spurious correlations between fluctuations in pupil diameter and band-limited power.
evidence: This is a statement about a potential confound, based on the cited reference.

claim: The pattern of correlations between pupil diameter and power remained largely unchanged after subtracting the fitted aperiodic component from the empirical power spectra.
source: The pattern of correlations between pupil diameter and power remained largely unchanged (Figure 6D):
evidence: This is a finding from a control analysis, supported by the data presented in Figure 6D.

claim: Fluctuations in pupil diameter were negatively correlated with activity in the low frequencies, around 4 Hz, as well as with activity in a higher frequency range around 32 Hz, after removing the aperiodic component.
source: Fluctuations in pupil diameter were negatively correlated with activity in the low frequencies, around 4 Hz, as well as with activity in a higher frequency range around 32 Hz.
evidence: This is a finding from a control analysis, supported by the data presented in Figure 6D.

claim: Band-limited activity in the range between 8 and 16 Hz exhibited robust positive correlations with pupil diameter after removing the aperiodic component.
source: Band-limited activity in the range between 8 and 16 Hz exhibited robust positive correlations.
evidence: This is a finding from a control analysis, supported by the data presented in Figure 6D.

claim: Correlations between residual power and pupil derivative were strongly reduced in magnitude and not significant for most frequencies after removing the aperiodic component.
source: Correlations between residual power and pupil derivative, on the other hand, were strongly reduced in magnitude and not significant for most frequencies (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from a control analysis, supported by the data presented in the supplementary figure.

claim: The couplings between pupil (and pupil-derivative) and band-limited cortical activity were genuine reflections of arousal-related modulations of periodic cortical activity with distinct effects for different frequency bands.
source: These control analyses confirm that the couplings between pupil (and pupil-derivative) and band-limited cortical activity reported in the preceding sections were genuine reflections of arousal-related modulations of periodic cortical activity with distinct effects for different frequency bands.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the control analysis.

claim: The study's findings are consistent with previously reported links between both locomotion-related and pupil-related changes in arousal and LFP recordings in sensory cortices of rodents.
source: Our findings are consistent with previously reported links between both locomotion-related and pupil-related changes in arousal and LFP recordings in sensory cortices of rodents (McGinley et al., 2015a; Reimer et al., 2014; Reimer et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement compares the study's findings to previous work in rodents.

claim: Periods of elevated arousal were accompanied by a decrease in low- and an increase in high-frequency activity, similar to cortical state changes typically observed during increased attention.
source: Briefly put, periods of elevated arousal were accompanied by a decrease in low- and an increase in high-frequency activity, similar to cortical state changes typically observed during increased attention (Harris and Thiele, 2011; Schwalm and Rosales Jubal, 2017).
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's findings, compared to previous work.

claim: The observed temporal relationships align with the lags between manipulations of arousal and pupil dilations of around 500–1000 ms in humans.
source: The observed temporal relationships also align with the lags between manipulations of arousal and pupil dilations of around 500–1000 ms in humans (Hoeks and Levelt, 1993; Wierda et al., 2012) and an ~500 ms delay between LC activation and peak pupil dilation in non-human primates (Joshi et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement compares the study's findings to previous work in humans and non-human primates.

claim: There is an ~500 ms delay between LC activation and peak pupil dilation in non-human primates.
source: The observed temporal relationships also align with the lags between manipulations of arousal and pupil dilations of around 500–1000 ms in humans (Hoeks and Levelt, 1993; Wierda et al., 2012) and an ~500 ms delay between LC activation and peak pupil dilation in non-human primates (Joshi et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited reference.

claim: In rodents, Reimer et al., 2016, and Breton-Provencher and Sur, 2019, reported peak correlations between noradrenergic axonal activity and pupil diameter at around 900 ms.
source: In rodents, Reimer et al., 2016, and Breton-Provencher and Sur, 2019, reported peak correlations between noradrenergic axonal activity and pupil diameter at around 900 ms, whereas the correlation between BF-regulated cholinergic activity and pupil diameter peaked around 500 ms (Reimer et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited references.

claim: The correlation between BF-regulated cholinergic activity and pupil diameter peaked around 500 ms in rodents.
source: In rodents, Reimer et al., 2016, and Breton-Provencher and Sur, 2019, reported peak correlations between noradrenergic axonal activity and pupil diameter at around 900 ms, whereas the correlation between BF-regulated cholinergic activity and pupil diameter peaked around 500 ms (Reimer et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited reference.

claim: The study reports comparable peak lags for low- (832 ms) and high-frequency activity (562 ms), suggesting that different neuromodulatory systems may drive correlations in different frequency ranges in the human brain.
source: Here, we report comparable peak lags for low- (832 ms) and high-frequency activity (562 ms), suggesting that different neuromodulatory systems may drive correlations in different frequency ranges in the human brain.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's findings and an interpretation.

claim: The low-frequency regime referred to in rodent work (2–10 Hz) includes activity that shares characteristics with human alpha rhythms (3–6 Hz).
source: The low-frequency regime referred to in rodent work (2–10 Hz; e.g., McGinley et al., 2015b) includes activity that shares characteristics with human alpha rhythms (3–6 Hz; e.g., Nestvogel and McCormick, 2022; Senzai et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited references.

claim: A negative correlation, localized to somatomotor cortices and specific to alpha-band (8–12 Hz) activity, peaked earlier than a positive correlation that localized to occipital visual cortices and encompassed alpha and beta bands.
source: Specifically, a negative correlation, localized to somatomotor cortices and specific to alpha-band (8–12 Hz) activity, peaked earlier than a positive correlation that localized to occipital visual cortices and encompassed alpha and beta bands (see Figures 3C and 4D).
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's findings.

claim: The effect in visual cortices had the shortest lag with respect to pupil dilation (~200 ms).
source: Of all effects found, the effect in visual cortices had the shortest lag with respect to pupil dilation (~200 ms).
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's findings.

claim: The short-lag positive correlation in visual cortices may stem from interactions between the LC and regions of the thalamus, in particular those implicated in the generation of occipital alpha-band activity via thalamo-cortical feedback loops (e.g., the pulvinar).
source: This short-lag positive correlation may stem from interactions between the LC and regions of the thalamus (McCormick, 1989; McCormick et al., 1991; Stitt et al., 2018), in particular those implicated in the generation of occipital alpha-band activity via thalamo-cortical feedback loops (e.g., the pulvinar; Saalmann et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the study's findings and previous work.

claim: Thalamo-cortical feedback loops may be sensitive to noradrenergic or even BF regulated cholinergic modulation.
source: These loops may therefore be sensitive to noradrenergic (Dahl et al., 2022) or even BF regulated cholinergic modulation (Nestvogel and McCormick, 2022; Zagha and McCormick, 2014).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the study's findings and previous work.

claim: The arousal-dependent low-lag alpha-/beta-band activity may be linked to the activity of a distinct subpopulation of GABAergic neurons in the LC, which have been shown to exhibit a temporally closer relationship with pupil diameter compared to the noradrenergic neurons.
source: Another, not mutually exclusive, possibility is that the arousal-dependent low-lag alpha-/beta-band activity is linked to the activity of a distinct subpopulation of GABAergic neurons in the LC, which have been shown to exhibit a temporally closer relationship with pupil diameter compared to the noradrenergic neurons (Breton-Provencher and Sur, 2019).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the study's findings and previous work.

claim: Previous work on task-related EEG and MEG dynamics reported a negative relationship between pupil-linked arousal and alpha-range activity in occipito-parietal sensors during visual processing and fear conditioning.
source: Seemingly contradicting the present findings, previous work on task-related EEG and MEG dynamics reported a negative relationship between pupil-linked arousal and alpha-range activity in occipito-parietal sensors during visual processing (Meindertsma et al., 2017) and fear conditioning (Dahl et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited references.

claim: Results from task-related experiments, that focus on evoked changes in pupil diameter rather than fluctuations in tonic pupil size, cannot be directly compared with the study's findings.
source: Note however that results from task-related experiments, that focus on evoked changes in pupil diameter rather than fluctuations in tonic pupil size, cannot be directly compared with our findings.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of comparing different types of studies.

claim: Similar to noradrenergic neurons in LC, phasic pupil responses exhibit an inverse relationship with tonic pupil size.
source: Similar to noradrenergic neurons in LC (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005), phasic pupil responses exhibit an inverse relationship with tonic pupil size (Knapen et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited references.

claim: On trials with larger baseline pupil diameter, the evoked (phasic) pupil response will be smaller and vice versa.
source: This means that on trials with larger baseline pupil diameter (e.g., during a pre-stimulus period), the evoked (phasic) pupil response will be smaller and vice versa.
evidence: This is a statement about the relationship between tonic and phasic pupil responses, based on the cited reference.

claim: A negative correlation between alpha-band activity in the visual cortex and task-related phasic pupil responses does not preclude a positive correlation with tonic pupil size during baseline or rest.
source: Therefore, a negative correlation between alpha-band activity in the visual cortex and task-related phasic pupil responses does not preclude a positive correlation with tonic pupil size during baseline or rest, as reported here.
evidence: This is a statement about the interpretation of the study's findings in relation to previous work.

claim: Whitmarsh et al., 2021, found a negative relationship between alpha-activity and pupil size in the somatosensory cortex that agrees with the study's finding.
source: In line with this, Whitmarsh et al., 2021, found a negative relationship between alpha-activity and pupil size in the somatosensory cortex that agrees with our finding.
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Reported changes in alpha activity in the visual cortex cannot be trivially explained by pupil dilation altering retinal illumination.
source: Note that reported changes in alpha activity in the visual cortex cannot be trivially explained by pupil dilation altering retinal illumination. In that case, one would expect a negative relationship, that is, decreasing alpha power with increasing pupil size (e.g., Donner and Siegel, 2011).
evidence: This is a statement about a potential confound and why it does not explain the study's findings.

claim: Changes in alpha activity preceded changes in pupil dilation, albeit with a shorter lag compared to activity in other frequency ranges.
source: Moreover, changes in alpha activity preceded changes in pupil dilation, albeit with a shorter lag compared to activity in other frequency ranges (see Figure 3).
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's findings.

claim: The temporal profile of the diverse relationships between pupil-linked arousal and local cortical activity may point toward a cascade of interrelated effects that the resting brain undergoes routinely.
source: The temporal profile of the diverse relationships between pupil-linked arousal and local cortical activity described above may point toward a cascade of interrelated effects that the resting brain undergoes routinely.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Episodes of arousal could arise seemingly at random, from underlying complex nonlinear neural dynamics.
source: Several scenarios could produce such a cascade: First, episodes of arousal could arise seemingly at random, from underlying complex nonlinear neural dynamics (Kringelbach and Deco, 2020; Robinson et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the origin of arousal episodes, supported by the cited references.

claim: Episodes of arousal could be coupled to other physiological processes, such as respiration.
source: Second, they could be coupled to other physiological processes, such as respiration (Kluger and Gross, 2021; Zelano et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the origin of arousal episodes, supported by the cited references.

claim: Respiration has an average base rate of ~0.2 Hz, similar to pupil fluctuations.
source: Respiration has an average base rate of ~0.2 Hz (Del Negro et al., 2018; Fleming et al., 2011), similar to pupil fluctuations (Bouma and Baghuis, 1971; Pomè et al., 2020; Turnbull et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited references.

claim: The observed cascade may imply a specific cognitive sequence: Most participants will likely have 'mind-wandered' or engaged in 'task-unrelated thoughts' while resting.
source: As a third scenario, the observed cascade may imply a specific cognitive sequence: Most participants will likely have 'mind-wandered' or engaged in 'task-unrelated thoughts' (Groot et al., 2021; Karapanagiotidis et al., 2020) while resting.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the cognitive state of participants during the resting-state recordings, supported by the cited references.

claim: The sequence of effects observed may be a transient re-orientation toward the external sensory environment – a 'monitoring sweep'.
source: The sequence of effects we observe may therefore be a transient re-orientation toward the external sensory environment – a 'monitoring sweep'.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the functional significance of the observed cascade.

claim: The increase in pupil-linked arousal, and its inverse relationship with an early dip in low-frequency activity, agrees with the cessation of a globally synchronized cortical state.
source: This is consistent with the increase in pupil-linked arousal, and its inverse relationship with an early dip in low-frequency activity, that is, the cessation of a globally synchronized cortical state, and agrees with a concurrent widespread increase in high-frequency cortical activity that signifies increased cortical excitability to process external sensory input (Hanslmayr et al., 2011; Harris and Thiele, 2011).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings, supported by the cited references.

claim: A concurrent widespread increase in high-frequency cortical activity signifies increased cortical excitability to process external sensory input.
source: This is consistent with the increase in pupil-linked arousal, and its inverse relationship with an early dip in low-frequency activity, that is, the cessation of a globally synchronized cortical state, and agrees with a concurrent widespread increase in high-frequency cortical activity that signifies increased cortical excitability to process external sensory input (Hanslmayr et al., 2011; Harris and Thiele, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited references.

claim: One aspect of mind-wandering is the retrieval of information from memory that heavily relies on theta rhythms in the hippocampus.
source: One aspect of mind-wandering is the retrieval of information from memory that heavily relies on theta rhythms in the hippocampus (Siegle and Wilson, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited reference.

claim: The study localized the strongest pupil (and pupil-derivative) correlations with theta-range power fluctuations in bilateral hippocampal regions, suggesting an arousal modulation of memory processes.
source: Here, we localized the strongest pupil (and pupil-derivative) correlations with theta-range power fluctuations in bilateral hippocampal regions (see Figure 4D), suggesting an arousal modulation of memory processes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Hippocampal LC-NE modulation has long been established in the rodent brain.
source: In support, hippocampal LC-NE modulation has long been established in the rodent brain (Sara, 2009; Segal and Bloom, 1976a; Segal and Bloom, 1976b), and McGinley et al., 2015a, reported negative correlations between pupil-linked arousal and the occurrence of theta-range hippocampal ripple events.
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited references.

claim: McGinley et al., 2015a, reported negative correlations between pupil-linked arousal and the occurrence of theta-range hippocampal ripple events.
source: In support, hippocampal LC-NE modulation has long been established in the rodent brain (Sara, 2009; Segal and Bloom, 1976a; Segal and Bloom, 1976b), and McGinley et al., 2015a, reported negative correlations between pupil-linked arousal and the occurrence of theta-range hippocampal ripple events.
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited reference.

claim: A recent human neuroimaging study found that pupil-linked arousal modulated blood oxygenation in (para-) hippocampal regions during memory processes.
source: Moreover, a recent human neuroimaging study found that pupil-linked arousal modulated blood oxygenation in (para-) hippocampal regions during memory processes (Clewett et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited reference.

claim: The observed sequence of effects concludes with a peak in alpha/beta activity that is triggered roughly at the time of maximum correlations of arousal with low- and high-frequency activity.
source: Further on, the observed sequence of effects concludes with a peak in alpha/beta activity that is triggered roughly at the time of maximum correlations of arousal with low- and high-frequency activity.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's findings.

claim: The increase in synchronized alpha/beta activity marks the return to a strong regime where external sensory (visual) input is attenuated, potentially indicating a shift to an introspective focus.
source: The increase in synchronized alpha/beta activity marks the return to a strong regime where external sensory (visual) input is attenuated, potentially indicating a shift to an introspective focus.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: A strong alpha rhythm imposes widespread bouts of 'pulsed inhibition' on visual cortex that suppress local gamma band activity.
source: A strong alpha rhythm thereby imposes widespread bouts of 'pulsed inhibition' on visual cortex that suppress local gamma band activity (Jensen and Mazaheri, 2010; Haegens et al., 2011; for a review, see Van Diepen et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited references.

claim: The relationship between alpha and gamma activity has been well described in non-human primate and human visual cortices, with a role for cholinergic neuromodulation.
source: This relationship between alpha and gamma activity has been well described in non-human primate (Spaak et al., 2012) and human visual cortices, with a role for cholinergic neuromodulation (Bauer et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited references.

claim: The study observed a decrease in local gamma-band activity in visual cortices.
source: Corroborating this scenario, we also observe a decrease in local gamma-band activity in visual cortices.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's findings.

claim: It remains possible that the sequence observed comprises independent effects with specific timings.
source: Further, it remains possible that the sequence we observe comprises independent effects with specific timings.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the study's interpretations.

claim: Kucyi and Parvizi, 2020, found spontaneous peaks of high-frequency band activity (>70 Hz) in the insular cortex of three resting surgically implanted patients that preceded pupil dilation by ~500 ms.
source: In fact, Kucyi and Parvizi, 2020, found spontaneous peaks of high-frequency band activity (>70 Hz) in the insular cortex of three resting surgically implanted patients that preceded pupil dilation by ~500 ms – a time range that is consistent with the lag of our cross-correlation between pupil size and high-frequency (>64 Hz) activity (see Figure 3B).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Kucyi and Parvizi, 2020, showed that the sequence of high-frequency activity preceding pupil dilation mimicked a similar but more pronounced pattern during task performance.
source: Importantly, they showed that this sequence mimicked a similar but more pronounced pattern during task performance.
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited reference.

claim: The finding of Kucyi and Parvizi, 2020, lends support to the idea that spontaneous covariations of pupil size and cortical activity signal arousal events related to intermittent 'monitoring sweeps' for behaviorally relevant information.
source: Given the purported role of the insula (Menon and Uddin, 2010), this finding lends support to the idea that spontaneous covariations of pupil size and cortical activity signal arousal events related to intermittent 'monitoring sweeps' for behaviorally relevant information.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings from Kucyi and Parvizi, 2020, in relation to the study's findings.

claim: Nonlinear relations between arousal and other factors are well characterized, most prominently in the form of the Yerkes-Dodson law.
source: Nonlinear relations between arousal and other factors are well characterized, most prominently in the form of the Yerkes-Dodson law, which posits an inverted U-shaped relation between arousal and cognitive performance (Yerkes and Dodson, 1908).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited reference.

claim: The Yerkes-Dodson law posits an inverted U-shaped relation between arousal and cognitive performance.
source: Nonlinear relations between arousal and other factors are well characterized, most prominently in the form of the Yerkes-Dodson law, which posits an inverted U-shaped relation between arousal and cognitive performance (Yerkes and Dodson, 1908).
evidence: This statement is supported by the cited reference.

claim: An inverted U relation has been identified for pupil-linked arousal fluctuations and detection performance and low-frequency (2–10 Hz) membrane potential fluctuations in primary auditory cortex.
source: More recently, an inverted U relation has also been identified for pupil-linked arousal fluctuations and detection performance and low-frequency (2–10 Hz) membrane potential fluctuations in primary auditory cortex (McGinley et al., 2015a).
